messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 54
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: North American
- Relationship Status: Married
- Occupation: Forester
- Trauma Type: Accidentally caused serious injury to another
- Pcl5: 52

# A Forester's Weight

Marcus has spent thirty-two years in the forest. He knows the smell of pine sap in summer, the particular quiet of snow-laden branches, the way light filters through Douglas firs at different times of day. He moves through the woods with the ease of someone who has made a life there, and his crew respects him—or did, before last June.

It was a Tuesday morning when everything changed. Marcus was supervising a crew of five younger men, clearing deadfall and thinning a stand near the ridge. He'd done this work thousands of times. The procedures were second nature: marking trees, positioning crew members, checking sight lines. But that morning, he made a calculation error. He misjudged the lean of a seventy-foot Douglas fir, underestimated how the wood would move as it fell.

The tree came down wrong. It twisted as it dropped, and one of the branches caught Danny Reeves across the legs. Marcus heard the sound—a crack and crunch that he still hears now, months later, at unexpected moments. Danny was airlifted to the regional hospital. Multiple fractures. Compartment syndrome. He kept both legs, but barely. He's had five surgeries. He won't walk without a cane, if he walks at all.

Marcus has not returned to the forest.

He sits in his home office now, ostensibly working on paperwork, but mostly staring out the window at the treeline beyond his property. His wife, Sarah, finds him there most mornings. He's lost fifteen pounds. His clothes hang differently. When she tries to talk to him about the investigation—which cleared him of negligence, which ruled it an accident—he nods but doesn't respond. His mind is somewhere else.

The nights are worst. Marcus lies awake beside Sarah, his body rigid, his mind replaying the moment over and over. Sometimes he dreams he's back there, but the tree never falls the way it should. It falls toward him instead, and he can't move. He wakes gasping, his heart pounding so hard he thinks it might break his ribs. Sarah reaches for him, but he flinches away. He can't bear to be touched.

During the day, sudden sounds trigger something in him. The crack of a branch, the rumble of a truck, even the sound of the neighbor's chainsaw sends electricity through his nervous system. His hands shake. His breath catches. He finds himself hypervigilant, scanning for danger, though the danger has already passed. It passed the moment Danny hit the ground.

What troubles Marcus most is the guilt that lives in his chest like a stone. He replays the morning endlessly, searching for the moment he could have done something differently. He should have called off the work. He should have positioned Danny differently. He should have been more careful, more precise, more something. The fact that the investigation concluded it was an accident, that his supervisor said these things happen, that other foresters have told him similar stories—none of it penetrates the conviction that he is responsible for Danny's suffering.

He's tried to visit Danny twice. Both times he sat in his truck in the hospital parking lot and couldn't make himself go inside. He imagined Danny's face, imagined the anger or pity or both. He couldn't face it. So he drives away, and the guilt deepens.

Sarah watches her husband withdraw further into himself each week. She doesn't recognize the man sitting in that office, staring at nothing. She recognizes his body, but something essential seems to have left him behind in the forest, trapped under that fallen tree.
